ནས་འབྲས་སོ་བའི་ཚད་ཡོངས་ཏེ། སྐྱེ་བོའི་ཚོགས་དེ་ལ་འབྲས་ཆང་པ་རེ་རེ་ཉི་མ་རེ་རེ་ཞིང་བྱིན་པར་གྱུར་ཏོ། །བདག་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་ཀྱང་ཆང་པ་གཉིས་མངོན་པར་འཚལ་བར་གྱུར་ཏོ། །སྐྱེ་བོའི་གྲངས་འཇུག་པར་གྱུར་པ་དེ་ལ་བྲམ་ཟེ་གཞན་དག་སྡོད་པར་མ་གྱུར་ཏོ། །དེས་ཀྱང་ཡུན་རིང་པོ་ནས་གཏམ་
དེ་ཐོས་ནས་ཉེ་བར་འོངས་ཏེ། བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་མདུན་དུ་སྡུག་བསྔལ་གྱིས་ཡོངས་སུ་ཕོངས་པའི་ཡི་གེ་འདི་སྨྲས་སོ། །རང་གི་སྐྱེ་བོའི་གྲོགས་དང་རྣམ་བྲལ་བས། །འདོད་པའི་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་མ་འོངས་པས། །སྣ་ཚོགས་རྒུད་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་སྐྱོན་གྱིས་ཀྱང་། །ཀྱེ་མ་འགྲོ་བ་གཏམ་ནི་
མང་བ་ཡིན། །བསྟན་པའི་སྡུག་བསྔལ་ཟིལ་གནོན་པའི། །སློང་བ་སྡུག་བསྔལ་ཆེན་པོའི་ཕྱིར། །ཡུན་རིང་ལམ་གྱིས་ཀུན་དུབ་པའི། །མདུན་དུ་རི་ལ་འཛེག་པ་ལྟར། །སྡུག་བསྔལ་བསྟན་པ་ཡིད་རེ་ང་། །འབྲས་བུ་མ་ཐོབ་སྐྱེ་བོ་ནི། །ཡུན་རིང་བྱ་བྱེད་འཆིང་བདག་གིས། །ཤིན་ཏུ་
འདི་ནི་སྡུག་བསྔལ་བྱེད། །བདེ་བའི་རེ་བའི་ཁྱིམ་རྨོངས་པས། །མཐོན་པོར་འཛེག་པའི་མི་རྣམས་ལ། །སྡུག་བསྔལ་སྐས་རིམ་ཕྲེང་བ་རྣམས། །མདུན་དུ་འཕེལ་བ་ཉིད་དུ་གྱུར། །འདི་ནི་མི་ལུས་སྡུག་བསྔལ་ཉིད། །སྐྱེ་བ་དང་ལྡན་འགག་པ་དང་། །དེ་ལྟ་ན་ཡང་རྨོངས་རྣམས་
ལ། །བདེ་པའི་འདུ་ཤེས་འཇུག་པར་གྱུར། །རྨོངས་པས་སེམས་ཀྱི་གླང་པོ་སྐྱོན། །དྲན་པའི་སྟོབས་ཀྱིས་ལྕགས་ཀྱུ་དོར། །དབང་པོའི་མཆེ་བ་གཉིས་རྣམས་ཀྱིས། །སྡུག་བསྔལ་རྒྱུ་ཡིས་{རིངས་,རིང་}ནས་ཕྲོགས། །སོ་གའི་དུས་ཀྱིས་གདུངས་པར་བྱས་པའི་རྨ་བྱ་ཡང་། །ས་ཡི་སྟེང་དུ་
གནས་པའི་ཆུ་ནི་འཐུང་མི་བྱེད། །ནམ་མཁའ་ལ་འཁོར་ཆར་དུས་སྐྱེས་ལ་སྡོད་པ་ནི། །ཁྱད་པར་འདོད་པའི་སྡུག་བསྔལ་སྟེན་བྱེད་སྐྱེ་བོ་ཡིན། །གལ་ཏེ་དབང་པོ་གཅིག་ལ་གནས་པར་བྱས་པར་གྱུར་ན་དེ་ཉིད་ལ་ནི་སྡུག་བསྔལ་འབྱུང་། །སྟོབས་དང་ལྡན་པ་གཅིག་གིས་ཀྱང་ནི་ཁུར་བོ་ཆེན་པོ་
ཁུར་བོར་ནུས་པ་མ་ཡིན་ཏེ། །དེ་ལྟར་ལྷ་ཡི་ལམ་གྱི་རྗེས་འབྲང་སྡུག་བསྔལ་ཤིན་ཏུ་ཆེ་བ་བདག་གིས་རྣམ་བསམས་ནས། །བདག་ཉིད་རྣམ་པ་དུ་མར་ཁྱབ་བདག་ཉིད་ཀྱིས་བྱས་ཏེ་དབང་པོ་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་ནི་གནས། །རྒྱལ་བོས་གསུངས་པ། བྲམ་ཟེ་ཆེན་པོ་བདག་ཉིད་ཀྱི་སྡུག་བསྔལ་འདི་ལྟར་

<meta>This page continues the narrative of a Bodhisattva king or leader practicing extreme generosity during a time of scarcity.</meta>

The amount of barley and rice was measured out, and to that gathering of people, one handful of grain was given every single day. The <term>Bodhisattva</term> <gloss>an awakened being dedicated to the benefit of others</gloss> himself also sought to survive on only two handfuls. While the number of people grew, other <term>Brahmins</term> <gloss>members of the priestly or scholarly caste</gloss> did not remain. Having heard the news from a long distance away, a certain man approached and, in the presence of the Bodhisattva, spoke these words regarding his complete destitution and suffering:

By being separated from the companions of my own people, 
And because the perfection of desires did not come, 
Even through the faults of various forms of decline, 
Alas, the talk among living beings is plentiful.

Because the suffering of begging, 
Which overwhelms the suffering that has been shown, is great, 
I am exhausted by the long road, 
Like climbing a mountain in front of me.

The display of suffering is terrifying. 
The person who has not obtained the fruit, 
Bound by long-standing actions and duties, 
Is made to suffer greatly by this.

For people who, through the delusion of a home of hopeful happiness, 
Climb to great heights, 
The successive steps of the ladder of suffering 
Increase directly before them.

This human body is itself suffering, 
Possessed of birth and cessation. 
Nevertheless, for those who are deluded, 
The perception of happiness arises.

Delusion stains the elephant of the mind. 
Through the power of mindfulness, the iron hook is cast away. 
By the two tusks of the senses, 
One is long ago robbed by the causes of suffering.

Even the peacock, tormented by the heat of the summer season, 
Does not drink the water that stays upon the ground. 
Waiting for the rainy season to arise while circling in the sky, 
Such is the person who relies on the suffering of desiring excellence.

If one were to reside within only a single sense organ, suffering would arise in that very place. Even a strong person is not able to carry a massive burden alone. Thus, having reflected on the extremely great suffering that follows the path of the gods, I have made myself pervasive in many ways and reside in all the senses.

The King said: Great Brahmin, regarding this suffering of yours...

<summary>A destitute Brahmin approaches a Bodhisattva leader during a famine to describe the inherent suffering of human existence and the burden of desire. The passage uses metaphors of elephants and peacocks to illustrate the struggle between mindfulness and sensory attachment.</summary>
<keywords>Bodhisattva, suffering, Brahmin, generosity, mindfulness, desire, famine, elephant metaphor</keywords>

དང་སྨ་ར་སེར་སྐྱ་དང་ལྡན་པ། བསྙུངས་པ་རྣམས་ཀུན་ནས་རིད་པའི་ལུས་མ་ཁྲོས་ཀྱང་ཁྲོས་པ་དང་འདྲ་བའི་བྲམ་ཟེ་སྲིན་པོའི་གཟུགས་དང་འདྲ་བའི་རིག་པ་སྨྲ་བ་དེ་མཐོང་ནས་འཇིགས་པའི་ཡིད་ཀྱིས་བསམ་ཞིང་གནས་སོ། །རིག་པ་འཛིན་པ་འདི་སྔགས་ཀྱི་མཐུས་ངེས་པར་བདག་ཁྱེར་བར་འདོད་པ་
སྟེ། དེ་ནི་དེ་བས་ན་གང་ལ་སྐྱབས་སུ་འགྲོ་སྙམ་དུ་རྣམ་པར་བསམས་ནས་སྐད་ཅིག་ཙམ་འོག་ཏུ་ལྟ་བས་ཀུན་ནས་གནས་པར་གྱུར་ཏོ། །ཆུ་རྟེན་དེ་དང་ཤིན་ཏུ་རིང་པོ་མ་ཡིན་པ་ན་དཀའ་ཐུབ་ཀྱིས་ཀུན་ནས་རིད་པའི་ལུས་དཀའ་ཐུབ་ཀྱི་ནོར་ཅན་སོ་སོར་གནས་པར་གྱུར་ཏེ། དཀའ་ཐུབ་ཀྱི་ནོར་ཅན་
དེ་ལ་ཡང་པདྨ་ཅན་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ཉ་ཤོར་བ་ཉེ་བར་འོངས་ནས་ཉི་མ་རེ་རེར་བསྙེན་བཀུར་བྱེད་པར་གྱུར་ཏོ། །དེ་ནས་ཀླུ་དེས་རིག་པ་སྨྲ་བ་དེ་ལ་ཉེ་བར་སྤྱོད་པའི་ཁྱིམ་ཐབ་གང་ཡིན་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་རྣམ་པར་སྤྱད་པར་གྱུར་ཏེ། རྒྱལ་པོ་འདི་ནི་འདི་ལ་སྐྱོབ་པར་མི་འགྱུར་ཏེ། །རིག་པ་གྲུབ་པ་ལས་ནི་དཀའ་ཐུབ་འདི་

His eyes were yellowish-gray like sparks of fire. His hair and beard were yellowish-gray, like the red tips of fully ripened grain. Though he was not angry, his body was completely emaciated from austerities, making him look like a wrathful <term>Brahmin</term> <gloss>priestly caste member</gloss> with the form of a <term>Rakshasa</term> <gloss>flesh-eating demon</gloss>. Seeing this scholar, the <note>Naga king</note> remained there with a terrified mind.

Thinking, "This <term>Vidyadhara</term> <gloss>Knowledge-holder or sorcerer</gloss> surely intends to capture me by the power of his <term>mantras</term> <gloss>sacred incantations</gloss>," he contemplated where to go for refuge. For a moment, he looked downward and remained still. Not very far from that body of water, there lived a man whose only wealth was his asceticism, his body completely withered by his penance. A fisherman named Padmaca used to come to that ascetic every day to pay his respects and offer service.

Then that <term>Naga</term> <gloss>serpent deity</gloss> considered who could serve as a protector against the scholar: "This king will not be able to protect me from him. This ascetic is also not the one, as the other has accomplished the <term>vidya</term> <gloss>magical knowledge</gloss>. Therefore, I will go to this fisherman who has found an opportunity, and quickly make a request."

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>the darkness of madness was cleared away. With a joyful mind, he took the ring and thought: 

->Today I have found the flower of my beloved’s tree, this ring. When shall I see the fruit of this discovery and find peace of mind?<-

Afterwards, he spoke to the sage: "Blessed One, I see that the suffering of my madness has been exhausted by this initiation of the water of instructions. Desires are like the <term>Kimpaka</term> <gloss>a fruit that is beautiful but poisonous when eaten</gloss> fruit; they produce a sweet taste while eating but result in suffering at the end. Who would sink themselves into the mud of desire? Even knowing how I experienced that pleasure, because I have not yet obtained my heart's captor, this is the reason:

->The minds of beautiful women, soft as flowers, are terrified by separation from their beloved. Their limbs are swooning from the poison of being parted from me. If that ascetic woman should truly cast away her life during the season of the trees because of me, and if I were to remain alive, what other person could be so devoid of compassion? Therefore, as long as she might cast away her life due to separation from me, I shall exert effort to reach her, urged on by compassion.<-

Then, speaking honestly to the sage, he took the letter, the ring, and the medicine known as the <term>Amrita</term> <gloss>nectar of immortality</gloss> medicine. He emerged from that hut of tree leaves and thought: "If I tell this story to my parents in any way, they will surely create obstacles to my going to the city of the <term>Kinnara</term> <gloss>mythical celestial musicians, half-human and half-horse or bird</gloss> king." 

Having considered this, he went slightly into another region. In the house of a friend, he ate the medicine prepared with clarified butter. He then took the lute on which the letter was written, along with two iron stakes, a hammer, a sword, and a quiver of arrows. Gradually, he crossed the Snowy Mountains <note>the Himalayas</note>, which were white like a mass of pearls, and reached the place called Bad-Bank <note>original: "འགྲམ་ངན་" (ngram ngan)</note>.

<summary>The protagonist recovers from madness after receiving instructions and a ring, then resolves to find his beloved Kinnari princess despite the dangers. He secretly prepares equipment and medicine before journeying across the Himalayas toward the celestial city.</summary>
<keywords>Kimpaka fruit, ascetic, Kinnara, Snowy Mountains, compassion, initiation, medicine</keywords>

བྱས་ནས། །ནམ་ཞིག་འོང་བར་གྱུར་ཏེ་བདག་མི་ཤེས། །ཞེས་ནས་ཡོངས་སུ་ཞུགས་སོ། །གང་གིས་འོངས་པ་དང་འདུག་པའང་མི་དྲན་པར་དགའ་བའི་གྲོགས་མོའི་བསྟི་གནས་སུ་ཕྱིན་ཏེ་བདག་ཉིད་ངོ་མཚར་ཆེ་ནས་རབ་ཏུ་ཞུགས་སོ། །འདིར་ཇི་ལྟར་སྦྲང་རྩི་བྱེད་པའི་རྐང་པའི་ཁུར་གྱིས་མེ་ཏོག་རབ་ཏུ་རྒྱས་པའི་
རྡུལ་གྱི་ཚོགས་པས་ཁྱབ་པའི་རྡོ་ལེབ་(གྱི་,ཀྱི་)སྟེང་ནཱ་ག་གེ་སར་གྱི་སྲང་ལམ་དུ་བྱས་པ་ལ་དགའ་བའི་གྲོགས་མོ་པདྨ་བ་ཏཱི་ནི་སྦྲང་གི་བུ་མོ་དང་ལྷན་ཅིག་ཏུ་གནས་ཤིང་ཅུང་ཟད་ཅུང་ཟད་སྨྲ་ཞིང་འཁོད་དེ། དྲུང་དུ་ཉེ་བར་ཉེ་བར་འོངས་སོ། །དེ་ནས་སྦྲང་གི་བུ་མོ་དང་པདྨ་ཅན་རབ་ཏུ་ཞུགས་ཏེ། པདྨ་ཅན་ནས། ཀྱེ་སྦྲང་
རྩིའི་བུ་མོ་བདག་གི་སྙིང་མྱོས་པ་སྙམ་བྱེད་དོ་ཞེས་དགའ་བའི་གྲོགས་མོ་རིན་ཆེན་ཕྲེང་བ་མ་ལ་ལྟ་བར་བྱེད་ཅིང་། ཅིའི་ཕྱིར་ན་དེ་ཙམ་དུ་ཡང་མི་འོང་བར་གྱུར། རིག་འཛིན་མས་ཉེ་བར་ཐོས་ནས་ཀྱེ་པདྨ་ཅན་སེམས་གཏོར་བར་མ་བྱེད་ཅེས་ཟེར། འདིར་དེ་དག་གཉིས་ན་རེ་ཨ་རེ་དགའ། ཨ་རེ་དགའ་ཞེས་སྨྲ་
ཞིང་གཉིས་པོ་རྟབ་རྟབ་པོར་ལངས་སོང་ནས། ཨ་ཨི་ཅི་ཡིན་ཅི་ཡིན་རིག་འཛིན་མ་ནས་ཀུན་གྱི་ལྟ་བྱེད་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་བལྟ་བར་འོས་པ་བདག་གིས་མཐོང་སྟེ་མིག་གིས་འབྲས་བུ་ཐོབ་བོ། །གཉིས་པོ་ནས་ཁྱོད་ཀྱིས་ཅི་མཐོང་སྨྲོས་ཤིག །རིག་འཛིན་ལ་ནི་སླར་ཡང་དེ་ཉིད་སྨྲ་བར་བྱེད་དོ། །གཉིས་པོས་ཡང་
འདྲི་ཞིང་རིག་འཛིན་མ་ལ་པདྨ་ཅན་རབ་ཏུ་འཁྱུད་དོ། །བདག་ནི་རབ་ཏུ་དགའ་བའི་གཞན་དབང་དུ་གྱུར་ཏེ། གལ་ཏེ་བདག་གིས་དབྱངས་ཅན་མ་ལ་བར་རྙེད་ན་སྨྲའོ། །གཉིས་པོ་ནས། ཁྱོད་ཀྱི་དགའ་བདེ་ཤིན་ཏུ་ལྕི་མོ་ཞིག་ཞུགས་པ་འདྲའོ། །རིག་འཛིན་མ་ནས་འདི་ནི་གཞན་མཐོང་ནས་ཀྱང་དེ་ལ་དགའ་བ་ཆེན་པོ་

Moving their lotus-like hands in a dance, the light from their garments touched the tips of their anklets in the sky, and they moved across the peaks of the snowy mountains. After saying, "We too shall accomplish our desires perfectly just as we wish," the two of them entered with certainty and remained facing forward.

Then the <term>Vidyadhari</term> <gloss>Knowledge-Holder woman; a female celestial being</gloss> entered. While dancing, she cried out: "Accitsira-am, Accitsira-am! <note>These appear to be phonetic renderings of ecstatic exclamations or mantras.</note> By whom could such a person on this great earth be seen, when even the gods find it difficult to behold? Having come under the power of another through great joy, I have entrusted my burden to my dear friend Padmavati. I do not know when I shall return!" With that, she fully entered.

Without even remembering her coming or going, she arrived at the dwelling of her dear friend in a state of great wonder and entered. Here, just like a honey-maker <note>a bee</note> burdened by its legs, she moved along a path of <term>Nagakesara</term> <gloss>a fragrant Himalayan flower, Mesua ferrea</gloss> onto a stone slab covered in heaps of pollen from fully bloomed flowers. There, the dear friend Padmavati sat with the "daughter of honey" <note>likely a maidservant or a specific companion named after a bee</note>, speaking softly. She approached closer and closer.

Then the "daughter of honey" and Padmini <note>original: "the one with the lotus"</note> entered. Padmini said, "O daughter of honey, my heart feels as if it is intoxicated," while looking for her dear friend Ratnamala <note>original: "the one with the jewel garland"</note>. "Why has she not come for so long?"

The <term>Vidyadhari</term> overheard this and said, "O Padmini, do not be distracted!"

The two of them exclaimed, "Oh, what joy! Oh, what joy!" and both rose up hurriedly. "Ah! What is it? What is it?"

The <term>Vidyadhari</term> replied, "I have seen that which is worthy of being seen by the eyes of all; my eyes have attained their fruit <note>the purpose of sight has been fulfilled</note>."

The two asked, "Tell us, what did you see?"

The <term>Vidyadhari</term> spoke of it to them again. As they questioned her further, Padmini embraced the <term>Vidyadhari</term> tightly.

"I have fallen under the power of a great joy," the <term>Vidyadhari</term> said. "If I find an opportunity to speak to Sarasvati <note>the goddess of eloquence and music</note>, I shall tell her."

The two replied, "It seems a very heavy joy and bliss has entered you."

The <term>Vidyadhari</term> said, "Even seeing another person, a great joy toward them..."

<summary>This page describes a scene of celestial or courtly joy where a Vidyadhari returns from a wonderous sighting to her friends Padmavati and Padmini. The dialogue captures their excitement and the intoxicated state of bliss following a significant encounter.</summary>
<keywords>Vidyadhari, Padmavati, Padmini, Nagakesara, Sarasvati, celestial dance, intoxication of joy</keywords>

འགྱུར། །ཁྱོད་ཀྱིས་བཏང་ནའང་ཇི་ལྟར་འགྱུར་བ་གཟིགས། །ངང་པ་མང་པོ་གྲགས་པའི་བདག་པོ་འདི། །ནམ་མཁའ་དངས་པའི་ནང་ན་རྣམ་མཛེས་པ། །ལྷ་མིན་རྒྱལ་པོ་ཟླ་བ་བཟང་པོ་བཞིན། །དེ་ནས་རྔོན་པ་དེ་སྙིང་སྲ་ཞིང་རྩུབ་པ་ལ་གོམས་ཀྱང་། དེ་རང་གི་སྲོག་ལ་ཡང་མི་བལྟ་
བར་ཇོ་བོ་ལ་སྙིང་ཉེ་ཞིང་བྱམས་པས་ཆུ་གང་ཁྲེལ་ལྟས་ཆེ་བའི་ཡོན་ཏན་གྱི་གཟི་བྱིན་དང་ལྡན་པ། བརྟན་ཞིང་འཇམ་པོར་སྨྲ་བའི་རྒྱན་གྱིས་བརྒྱན་པའི་ཚིག་དེས་སེམས་དུལ་བར་གྱུར་ནས་ངོ་མཚར་ཆེ་ཞིང་རབ་ཏུ་གུས་པའི་དབང་གིས་ཐལ་མོ་སྦྱར་ཏེ་བཞིན་བཟང་ལ་སྨྲས་པ། སྐལ་བ་ཆེན་
པོ་ལེགས་སོ་ལེགས་སོ། །ཇོ་བོའི་དོན་དུ་སྲོག་བཏང་བ། །ཁྱོད་ཀྱིས་འདིར་ནི་གང་བསྟན་པ། །དེ་ལྟ་བུ་ཡི་ཆོས་བཟང་བ། །མི་འམ་ལྷ་ཡི་ནང་ན་དཀོན། །དེ་བས་ཁྱོད་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་པོ་དེ། །མགུ་བར་བྱས་ནས་གཏང་བར་བྱའོ། །ཁྱོད་ཀྱི་སྲོག་པས་ཕོངས་དེ་ལ། །གནོད་པ་བྱེད་པ་

<meta>The text continues from the previous page's narrative regarding the capture of the Hamsa king and the loyalty of his minister Sumukha.</meta>

Neither of us will lose or win. If you do not trust me, then first take hold of me and let the King of Birds go later. Your gain will remain the same, and I ask that you grant my request. This will also please the many geese and strengthen our friendship. Look at what happens if you release him. This Master of Many Geese, famous and renowned, is as beautiful within the clear sky as the <term>Asura</term> <gloss>demigod</gloss> King <term>Vimala</term> <gloss>the Moon</gloss>.

Then, although that hunter was accustomed to a hard and cruel heart, his mind was subdued by those words. These were words adorned with the ornament of firm and gentle speech, possessing the majestic brilliance of qualities like modesty and shame, spoken by one who was affectionate and loving toward his lord, disregarding even his own life. Being greatly amazed and moved by deep respect, he pressed his palms together and spoke to <term>Sumukha</term> <gloss>the Good-Faced One</gloss>:

"Great fortunate one, well done, well done! The noble conduct you have shown here, giving your life for the sake of your lord, is rare even among humans or gods. Therefore, having been pleased by you, I shall release your King. Who would dare to harm one who cherishes your life so dearly?"

Having said this, the hunter followed the command of that official <note>referring to Sumukha</note>. Showing great respect to the compassionate King of Geese, he untied the snare and set him free. Then <term>Sumukha</term>, the leader of the geese, was filled with joy in his heart because the King of Geese had been released. Looking at the hunter with a gaze of joy and affection, he said:

"Just as I, his friend, have become joyful because you released the King of Geese, may you, my friend, also be very joyful together with your kinsmen for many hundreds of autumns! So that the work you have done does not become fruitless, take both me and the Master of Many Geese comfortably upon your carrying pole and present us before the King in the palace. Upon seeing the King of Geese together with his servant, that King will surely be delighted. Great treasures to satisfy you will also..."

<summary>Sumukha convinces the hunter to release the Goose King by offering himself in exchange, leading the moved hunter to free the captive. Sumukha then suggests they visit the human King voluntarily so the hunter may be rewarded for his compassion.</summary>
<keywords>Hamsa Jataka, Sumukha, compassion, loyalty, sacrifice, hunter, King of Geese</keywords>

Then, because of that extraordinary flavor, 
The king was filled with great wonder.
Just as the supreme quality of its prepared excellence 
Matches its marvelous and supreme taste,
So by its unprecedented color and fragrance, 
He was filled with great wonder.
Through his attachment to its flavor,
He became completely overcome by wonder.

Then, although that king possessed an abundance of delicious and perfect foods, because he was under the power of attachment to that specific flavor, he thought to himself:

"For one who has not eaten these fruits, 
What kind of 'fruit' of kingship has he truly tasted?
Even without the afflictions of managing a kingdom,
One who eats such as this is a true king."

Then, he thought to search for where the fruit had come from, and he reasoned with his own intellect: "The excellent tree from which such a fruit comes must be located not far from here, and it is undoubtedly on the bank of the river."

If one asks how this is evident: "Looking at how the color, fragrance, and taste are unimpaired, and seeing that it is without bruises or injuries, it seems it has not been long since it fell into the water. Therefore, I am perfectly able to know the place from where this originated."

Having thought this, and being under the power of attachment to that flavor, he set out to play in that water <note>or to follow the course of the river</note>. ཕུལ་བ་རྣམས་བླངས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདིས་ནི་ལེན་པ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །གཉེན་དང་མཛའ་བཤེས་རྟེན་དང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ལ་སོགས་པས་ནི་སྦྱིན་པ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །བྲམ་ཟེ་ལས་སུ་བསྟན་པས་ལས་ལྷག་མ་ཅི་ཞིག་ལུས་ཤེ་ན། མཆོད་སྦྱིན་བྱེད་དུ་འཇུག་པ་སྟེ། དེ་ནི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའ་
མི་མཛད་དེ། འགྲོ་བ་ཐམས་ཅད་ལ་འཚེ་བ་མེད་པ་དང་ལྡན་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཏེ། འཚེ་བ་སྤོང་བར་འདོད་པས་སོ། །མཉེན་དང་མཛའ་བཤེས་རྟེན་དང་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ལས་དང་གསོ་དགོས་པའི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་པའོ། །ཕོངས་པ་རྣམས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་སྙིང་རྗེའི་ཞིང་གི་དབང་དུ་བྱས་
པའོ། །མགྲོན་དང་བཀུར་སྟི་བྱ་བ་རྣམས། །ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ནི་ཡོན་ཏན་གྱི་ཞིང་སྟེ་མགྲོན་ཡང་ཡོན་ཏན་གྱི་ཞིང་དུ་གཟུང་བར་བྱ་སྟེ། གང་གི་ཕྱིར་སློང་བ་དག་ནི་བྱང་ཆུབ་སེམས་དཔའི་དགེ་བའི་བཤེས་གཉེན་དུ་གཟུང་བར་བྱའོ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཚིག་གིས་སོ། །བླ་མ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་
ནི་ཕན་འདོགས་པའི་ཞིང་ངོ་། །ཟླ་བ་ལྟ་བུ་ནི་མཁས་པར་གྲགས་པའོ། །སྟོན་ཀ་ལྟ་བུ་ནི་གཏོང་བ་དང་དཔའ་བའོ། །བྱ་བ་ངན་པས་བྲེལ་པའི་ཉེས་པས་གླགས་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བས་ནི་མངོན་པར་མཐོ་བའི་ཕྱོགས་དང་འགལ་བར་བསྟན་ཏོ། །བག་མེད་པའི་གནས་སུ་གྱུར་པ་
ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདིས་ནི་ངེས་པར་ལེགས་པ་དང་འགལ་བར་བསྟན་ཏོ། །བག་མེད་པ་གང་ཞེ་ན། དགེ་བའི་ཆོས་རྣམས་མི་སྒོམ་པ་སྟེ། འདིས་ནི་ཉོན་མོངས་པའི་ཀུན་ནས་ཉོན་མོངས་པས་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་ཉིད་དུ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །སྔ་མས་ནི་ལས་ཀྱི་ཀུན་ནས་ཉོན་མོངས་པས་ཉོན་མོངས་པ་ཉིད་དུ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །

<meta>continues from previous page</meta>What is signified by that is the characterization through completely pure conduct and qualities. The phrase being an ornament upon the earth refers to being born into a high and noble lineage. Because he was exceedingly and exceptionally beautiful, he became an ornament. The phrase having performed the deeds of a man <note>original: "skyes pa'i las"</note> and so forth refers to the performance of Vedic sacrifices <term>yajña</term> <gloss>ritual offerings or sacrifices</gloss>. The phrase having studied the Vedas along with their branches refers to the mastery of recitation and study. The phrase his fame for wisdom filled the world of men refers to his role in instructing others in recitation.

The phrase having accepted what was offered refers to receiving gifts <term>dāna</term> <gloss>the act of receiving appropriate offerings as a priest</gloss>. The phrase toward kinsmen, friends, and dependents and so forth refers to the act of giving. One might ask: since these are shown as the duties of a Brahmin, what remaining duty is left? It is the duty of causing others to perform sacrifices. However, the Bodhisattva <gloss>a being dedicated to awakening for the sake of others</gloss> does not do this, because he possesses non-violence toward all living beings and desires to abandon harm.

The phrase toward kinsmen, friends, and dependents concerns those who are connected through karma or those who require support. The phrase those who are destitute concerns the field of compassion <note>a "field" is a recipient through whom one cultivates merit</note>. The phrase guests and those to be honored refers to the field of qualities. Guests should also be considered a field of qualities because of the saying: one should regard those who beg as the spiritual friends <term>kalyāṇamitra</term> <gloss>virtuous friends or guides</gloss> of a Bodhisattva. The term gurus <gloss>teachers or elders</gloss> refers to the field of benefactors.

The phrase like the moon refers to his fame for wisdom. The phrase like autumn refers to his generosity and courage. The phrase beset by the fault of being occupied with evil deeds shows the contradiction with the side of higher rebirth <term>abhyudaya</term> <gloss>prosperity or high status in future lives</gloss>. The phrase became a place of heedlessness shows the contradiction with definite goodness <term>niḥśreyasa</term> <gloss>liberation or the final good</gloss>. What is heedlessness? It is the failure to cultivate virtuous qualities. This shows the state of being afflicted through the corruption of the mental afflictions <term>kleśa</term> <gloss>disturbing emotions such as greed or anger</gloss>. The previous point shows the state of being afflicted through the corruption of karma <gloss>intentional actions and their results</gloss>.

<summary>This page provides a detailed commentary on the qualities and social duties of a Brahmin Bodhisattva, distinguishing between traditional Vedic obligations and the Buddhist principle of non-violence. It explains the various types of people who serve as fields for merit, such as the destitute and spiritual teachers.</summary>
<keywords>Brahmin, Bodhisattva, non-violence, sacrifice, generosity, fields of merit, heedlessness, karma, mental afflictions</keywords>

དེའི་མིང་ཇི་སྐད་དུ་བཏགས་ཤེ་ན། བཟོད་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་མིང་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེའི་མིང་ཡོན་ཏན་དང་ལྡན་པ་ཉིད་དུ་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར་སྨྲས་པ། ཡོན་ཏན་གྱིས་མངོན་པར་བསྒྲུབས་པ་ཉིད་དུ་མཛེས་པའི་མིང་གང་ཡིན་པ་དེ་ནི་ཡོན་ཏན་མངོན་བསྒྲུབས་བཟོད་པ་སྟེ། མཛེས་པའི་མིང་བདག་དང་། གཞན་གཉི་
ག་ལ་མཛེས་པའི་ཕྱིར་བཟོད་པའོ། །འཇིག་རྟེན་གྱི་དོན་བྱེད་པ་ནི། འཇིག་རྟེན་ལ་ཕན་པར་བྱེད་པ་སྟེ། འདིས་ནི་གཞན་ལ་ཕན་པའི་རྒྱུ་ཉིད་དུ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །སྙིང་རྗེས་བཀའ་སྩལ་ཅེས་བྱ་བ་ནི། སྙིང་རྗེ་ཅན་གྱི་བཀའ་ཡིན་པས་སྙིང་རྗེས་བཀའ་སྩལ་པའོ། །འདོད་ཆགས་མེད་པའི་རང་
བཞིན་དང་། འདོད་ཆགས་མེད་པའི་མཚན་ཉིད་བཟོད་པ་གཞན་གྱི་དོན་བྱེད་པར་འཇུག་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། དེ་ལྟར་བཟོད་པའི་རྒྱུ་བསྟན་ཏོ། །བསོད་ནམས་གྲགས་པ་དག་ཀྱང་རབ་ཏུ་འཕེལ། །ཞེས་བྱ་བ་དེའི་དོན་རྗེས་སུ་བསྟན་པ་ནི་མ་བཤད་དེ། དེ་བས་དེའི་རྒྱུ་ཟིལ་གྱིས་མནན་པས་བཟོད་པས་སྡིག་
པ་སྤོང་བ་ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཚིགས་བཅད་དེར་བསྟན་ཟིན་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཆུ་ཡིས་མ་བཀྲུས་པར་ཡང་དག་པར་འགྱུར། །ཞེས་བྱ་བ་འདིའི་རྗེས་སུ་བསྟན་པ་ནི། མཐུ་དང་ལྡན་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་རྒྱན་ཡང་ཡིན། །ཞེས་བྱ་བའི་ཚིགས་བཅད་འདིས་བསྟན་ཏེ། གང་དག་འདི་རྣམ་པར་དག་པར་བྱེད་པ་ཡིན་
ཞེ་ན། དེ་བསྟན་པའི་ཕྱིར་ཚིགས་བཅད་འདི་སྨོས་ཏེ། ཁྱིམ་པ་དང་། རབ་ཏུ་བྱུང་བ་རྣམས་ཀྱིའོ། །ཁྱིམ་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་ནི། མཐུ་དང་ལྡན་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱི་རྒྱན་ཡང་ཡིན། །ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ཡིན་ཏེ། གནོད་སེམས་ཀྱིས་དགོན་པའི་མེ་ལ་ཆུ་རྒྱུན་འབེབས་པའོ། །དཀའ་ཐུབ་ཅན་གྱི་སྟོབས་
མཆོག་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས་པ་ཡོད་ན་ནི། གནོད་སེམས་དགོན་པའི་མེ་ལ་ཆུའི་རྒྱུན་འབེབས་པ་ཡིན་ཏེ། གནོད་སེམས་ཀྱི་དགོན་པའི་མེ་ལ་ཆུའི་རྒྱུན་འབེབས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ཡིན་ཏེ། གནོད་སེམས་ཀྱི་དགོན་པའི་མེ་ལ་ཆུའི་རྒྱུན་དང་འདྲ་བར་དེ་ཉེ་བར་ཞི་བ་སྟེ། དེ་བས་ན་གནོད་སེམས་དགོན་པའི་མེ་
ལ་ཆུ་རྒྱུན་འབེབས་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ཡིན་ནོ། །དེའི་ཕྱིར། གཉི་གའི་ཚེ་ལ་དོན་མེད་ཞི་བར་བྱེད། །ཅེས་བྱ་བ་སྨོས་ཏེ། དེ་བས་ན་ཆུ་ཡིས་མ་བཀྲུས་པར་ཡང་དག་པར་བྱེད་དེ། དོན་མེད་པར་ཉེ་བར་ཞི་བར་བྱེད་པའི་ཕྱིར་རོ། །ཡོན་ཏན་དེ་དང་དེ་དག་ཕུན་སུམ་ཚོགས། །ཞེས་བྱ་བ་དེའི་རྗེས་སུ་བསྟན་པ་ནི།

If you ask what his name was given to be: his name was "Patience" <term>Kshanti</term> <gloss>forbearance or patience</gloss>. To show that his name was endowed with positive qualities, it is said: whatever name is made beautiful by being accomplished through virtues is "Patience Accomplished by Virtue." Because this beautiful name is attractive to both oneself and others, he is called Patience.

To "act for the sake of the world" means to act for the benefit of the world. This shows that he is the very cause of benefit for others. The phrase "spoken with compassion" means that because it is the speech of one possessing compassion, it is spoken with compassion.

The nature of being free from attachment and the characteristic of being free from attachment is for Patience to engage in acting for the sake of others. In this way, the cause of patience is shown.

Regarding the phrase "merit and fame also greatly increase," the subsequent explanation of its meaning is not explicitly stated here. This is because the verse explaining how patience abandons sin by overwhelming its cause has already been taught.

The phrase "completely purified even without being washed by water" is followed by this explanation: "It is also the ornament of those who possess power." To show who it is that this purifies, this verse is spoken: it refers to both householders and those who have gone forth <note>ordained monastics</note>.

For householders, it is "also the ornament of those who possess power." This is like pouring a stream of water onto the forest fire of malice. If there is the supreme excellence of the strength of an ascetic, it pours a stream of water onto the forest fire of malice. "Pouring a stream of water onto the forest fire of malice" means that it pacifies that fire of malice just like a stream of water. Therefore, it is called "pouring a stream of water onto the forest fire of malice."

Because of that, the phrase "it pacifies what is meaningless for the lives of both" is spoken. Therefore, it purifies without the use of water, because it pacifies what is meaningless. The subsequent explanation of the phrase "endowed with those various virtues" follows.

<summary>This text explains the symbolic and practical meaning of the name Patience, describing it as a virtuous quality that benefits both self and others while pacifying anger like water extinguishing a forest fire. It highlights that patience serves as a spiritual ornament for both laypeople and monastics by removing the harms of malice.</summary>
<keywords>Patience, Kshanti, compassion, virtue, merit, purification, malice, householders, monastics, asceticism</keywords>

Even now, the remaining results of those past deeds <note>The text refers to the ripening of karma from previous lifetimes.</note> are applied through the lies of the daughter of an ascetic <note>original: "tirthya" referring to a non-Buddhist sect</note>. Long ago, in the city of Bandhumati, the Blessed One, the Victorious Vipashyin <note>The 19th Buddha of the 27 Buddhas of the past</note>, resided while being honored with the enjoyments of the townspeople and surrounded by the assembly of monks.

A Brahmin named Mathara <note>original: "maṭhara"</note>, upon seeing him receiving such honors, said to the townspeople: "These shaven-headed monks are not worthy of such enjoyments. Prepare their food from the dust of <term>kotara</term> <gloss>a type of coarse grain or chaff</gloss> barley. The mouths of these shaven-headed ones, with such distorted appearances, are not worthy of divine food."

Because of those words, that Brahmin experienced the results of that sin through many births. Even now, due to the remainder of those deeds, I have eaten the food of <term>kotara</term> barley <note>referring to the Buddha's own experiences of hardship due to past speech karma</note>.

In a former time, when I was a Brahmin youth named Uttara, I obtained non-virtue by slandering a supreme lineage. Because of that deed, I have now performed six years of difficult ascetic practices.

<summary>This page recounts how the Buddha's current hardships, specifically eating coarse grain and undergoing six years of austerities, are the results of insulting enlightened beings in past lives as a Brahmin.</summary>
<keywords>Karma, Vipashyin Buddha, Bandhumati, Mathara, Uttara, asceticism, speech karma, barley</keywords>

<meta>The text is a Sanskrit-to-Tibetan translation of the Avadanakalpalata, a classic work of Buddhist literature by the Kashmiri poet Kshemendra. The page contains verses in both the original Sanskrit (transliterated into Tibetan script) and the Tibetan translation, following the traditional bilingual format.</meta>

Sanskrit Verse: <term>Bhāvaṃ</term> <gloss>The state or feeling</gloss>. Who has won the affection of the one who is expert in the arts, who is cooled by the accomplishment of the welfare of others? Have you seen the peahen who looks like the flash of a tender lightning bolt amidst the clouds? Even your own beautiful tail, which is made of merit, is wondrous to behold.

Tibetan Verse: Who can make the face of the one who is expert in the arts, cooled by the accomplishment of the welfare of others, shine? The one whose tresses and garlands are colorful and diverse, whose fame is like the collection of your own tail feathers. Have you, O peacock, seen her anywhere, that ground of beautiful clouds illuminated by lightning?

Sanskrit Verse: Have you seen any <term>bhujangi</term> <gloss>serpent-woman</gloss> with a supreme jewel upon her crown? Look! The rays of poison she emitted are burning me in this unbearable separation. O <term>saranga</term> <gloss>deer</gloss>, have you seen that playful woman of the King of Desire <note>the God of Love, Kamadeva</note>?

Tibetan Verse: Have you anywhere seen a serpent-woman possessing a supreme jewel upon her crown? Look! Because of the rays of poison she emitted, I am burned here by this unbearable separation. O deer, have you seen that woman who is the playmate of the God of Love? 

Sanskrit Verse: I think the eyes of the forest-deer shine through the distribution of her sidelong glances. O Lord of the Forest, have you seen that woman like a creeper at the forest’s edge, with lips as tender as new leaves, born of a place of wandering, moving with playful grace, her breasts like clusters of flowers?

Tibetan Verse: I think the forest-deer are made beautiful by the blue lotus of her sidelong glances. O Lord of the Forest, have you seen her at the forest’s edge, like a creeper, that woman with lips as beautiful as young leaves, moving with shifting grace, her hair like clusters of blossoms? Truly she is like a cloud of the forest thicket...

<summary>This page contains poetic verses from Kshemendra's Avadanakalpalata, where a protagonist in distress addresses elements of nature—peacocks, deer, and the forest itself—searching for a lost beloved. The language uses classical Sanskrit metaphors comparing female beauty to lightning, creepers, and jewels.</summary>
<keywords>Kshemendra, Avadanakalpalata, Buddhist poetry, Sanskrit literature, metaphors of nature, separation, serpent-woman</keywords>

<meta>This page contains a bilingual Sanskrit-Tibetan text from Kshemendra's Avadanakalpalata, specifically the conclusion of the 76th chapter and the beginning of the 77th chapter.</meta>

<note>original Sanskrit: nām tāvaḥ kvāpi praśama kusunā rāma bhājaṃ jagāma | iti kṣemendra viracitāyāṃ bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatāyāṃ vidurāvadānaṃ ṣaṭasaptatatamaḥ pallavaḥ</note>
The distress of those possessing the delightful garden of flowers of complete peace went somewhere away. Thus ends the 76th leaf <note>chapter</note> titled the Legend of Vidura from the *Vine of the Bodhisattva Legends* <note>original: Bodhisattvavadana-kalpalata</note> composed by Kshemendra <note>original: dge ba'i dbang po</note>.

<note>original Sanskrit: khalo-tkarṣeṇa sarvasya guṇa lagnā niḥprajāyate | bhavatya-bhudayāyai-va prabhā-vastu mahātmanām</note>
Through the dominance of the wicked, the qualities of everyone are impaired. However, through the power of the Great Souls, prosperity and advancement indeed come to pass.

<note>original Sanskrit: ātra māyāṃ vanopānte bhagavānsugataḥ purā | bhūtāgara guhāgarbhata-sthaudhyāna pārāyaṇaḥ</note>
Long ago, the Blessed One, the Sugata <gloss>Gone to Bliss</gloss>, remained focused on meditation within a cave that was a dwelling for spirits, at the edge of the Atramaya forest. 

<note>original Sanskrit: tatra tīvrāśani sphoṭa niṣpaṣṭa vṛṣa karṣakaḥ | tena dhyānalinena ghana śabdopi na śrutaḥ</note>
There, a violent lightning strike crushed a bull and a farmer. Yet, because he was absorbed in meditation, he did not even hear the sound of the thunderclouds.

<note>original Sanskrit: dhyānānte-tha pravacanaṃ śāstur-mandākinī taṭe | caturaḥ śrotum-ājagmar-mahārājā bhidhāḥ pura</note>
Then, at the conclusion of his meditation, on the banks of the Mandakini <gloss>the slow-flowing Ganges</gloss>, the four who are called the Great Kings came forward to hear the speech of the Teacher.

<note>original Sanskrit: dhṛtarāṣṭra virūḍhākhya virūpākṣa dhanādhipāḥ | te</note>
They were Dhritarashtra <gloss>Defender of the Realm</gloss>, Virudhaka <gloss>Noble Birth</gloss>, Virupaksha <gloss>Deformed Eyes</gloss>, and the Lord of Wealth <note>Vaishravana</note>. They...

<summary>This page concludes the Legend of Vidura and begins a new chapter describing the Buddha's deep meditative absorption in the Atramaya forest, so profound that he fails to hear a fatal lightning strike nearby. The Four Heavenly Kings approach the Buddha on the banks of the Ganges to receive his teachings.</summary>
<keywords>Kshemendra, Avadanakalpalata, Vidura, Buddha, meditation, Four Heavenly Kings, Dhritarashtra, Virudhaka, Virupaksha, Vaishravana</keywords>

By those <note>offerings</note>, he became like a wish-fulfilling tree to beggars, and his house was completely filled with a collection of pearls and gems. Once, having returned from another Isle of Jewels <term>Ratnadvipa</term> <gloss>an island famed in Sanskrit literature as a source of precious stones</gloss>, he went to visit the King, bringing a pearl necklace as a gift. The King rose to meet him and honored him with great affection. 

As if it were the laughing play of the Goddess of Fortune <term>Sri</term> <gloss>Lakshmi</gloss>, he offered that brilliant necklace to him. Like a cluster of stars strung together on a radiant thread, that necklace of excellent qualities captivated the heart of the King. 

At that moment, the King's young daughter, Sarasvati, entered the palace chambers and sang a verse of eloquent speech <term>subhashita</term> <gloss>well-spoken words or moral aphorisms</gloss>. Having heard that well-spoken verse, which was like nectar to the ears, the householder was so moved that the hairs on his body stood on end like sprouting shoots. In that state of rapture, he returned to his own home. Thereafter, he abandoned all food and pleasure, for his mind had been stolen by that elegant speech.

<summary>A wealthy householder presents a magnificent pearl necklace to the King, but is ultimately more captivated by a verse of elegant wisdom spoken by the King's daughter, Sarasvati.</summary>
<keywords>pearl necklace, Ratnadvipa, King, Sarasvati, elegant speech, subhashita, devotion</keywords>

As the supreme youth, may you completely pacify the pleasure of desire and obtain the state of the Lord of Victors. May you pacify the birth, death, and terror of the assembly of sentient beings afflicted by the mental poisons. May you attain the state that transcends the world, where even the name of fear is pacified, and which is free from the faults of aging.

The Letter to a Friend <note>original: "Suhrllekha"</note> sent by the master, the noble Nagarjuna <note>a foundational philosopher of the Middle Way school</note>, to his friend, King Gautamiputra <note>original: "bde spyod", identified as a king of the Satavahana dynasty</note>, is hereby complete. It was translated, edited, and finalized by the Indian abbot Sarvajñadeva and the chief editor and translator, the monk Paltssek <note>original: "ban de dpal brtsregs", a famous eighth-century Tibetan translator</note>.

# The Letter to a Disciple

In the language of India: <term>Shishyalekha</term>
In the language of Tibet: <term>Slob ma la spring ba'i spring yig</term> <gloss>The Letter to a Disciple</gloss>

Homage to the Three Jewels <note>the Buddha, his teaching, and the spiritual community</note>.

When the Kinnaras <note>celestial musicians, half-human and half-horse or bird</note> and goddesses recount his former deeds of extreme hardship, the faces of the daughters of Mara <note>the personification of death and desire</note> close up like a forest of lotuses touched by the rays of the moon.

He possesses a body that is auspicious, beautiful, and utterly wonderful. He is difficult to be seen by those with little merit. He fulfills the hopes and desires of the world, acting for the sake of others with a single intent, like a wish-fulfilling jewel.

He is one who always feels joy through the joy of others and feels great distress when others suffer. Having cultivated qualities through great compassion, he remains by setting aside his own pleasure and pain.

Even when giving away his heads for the sake of others, he looks on with eyes as wide and joyful as a lotus. For his own sake, he considers even the earth covered by a single white parasol as though it were the sharp edge of a sword.

His qualities are perfect and clear like the waxing moon. He is the unique and beautiful one who clears away the darkness of faults. He has appeared with great clarity, striving for the benefit of the world. Like the rising moon, he brings cooling relief to all living beings.

He upholds the supreme, precious teaching that is excellent and without decline. Those who are great accept the way of pure conduct with devotion, wearing it like a crown ornament, just like the expanded hood of a Naga king <note>serpent deity</note>.

<summary>This page concludes the Letter to a Friend by Nagarjuna and begins the Letter to a Disciple by Chandragomin. The new text opens with verses of praise for the Buddha's compassionate deeds and his dedication to the welfare of others.</summary>
<keywords>Nagarjuna, Gautamiputra, Chandragomin, Letter to a Disciple, compassion, merit, Three Jewels, Bodhisattva deeds</keywords>

if one generates desire for possessions, then that becomes <term>covetousness</term> <gloss>the mental intent to possess what belongs to others</gloss>. How is it <term>malice</term> <gloss>harmful intent</gloss>? If one harbors hatred toward other sentient beings, then that becomes malice. How does it become <term>wrong view</term> <gloss>distorted perspective</gloss>? If one thinks with certainty that there are no results of virtuous and non-virtuous actions <note>denying the law of cause and effect or karma</note>, then that becomes wrong view.

The distinction of sin in these three paths of mental action is known solely through the distinction of intention. Regarding covetousness, the distinction of sin is also considered to be by power of the object. By way of abandoning these ten paths of non-virtuous action, one should cultivate the ten paths of virtuous action.

Regarding the phrase, "Turn away from alcohols," although alcohol is indeed a cause of great <term>transgressions</term> <gloss>faults or downfalls</gloss>, the act of consuming it is not inherently non-virtuous in the same way as the other paths of action. Therefore, it is not explained within the primary paths of action but is taught as a separate prohibition. The plural term <note>referring to various types of intoxicants</note> is used because, while there is no difference in their capacity to cause intoxication, they are distinguished by their primary ingredients. 

Manufactured alcohols are of three types: 
1. Molasses alcohol 
2. Rice flour alcohol 
3. Honey alcohol 

Prepared alcohols should be understood as those produced by pressing flowers and similar methods.

The phrase, "Delight in a virtuous livelihood," should be connected to the instruction "to act." A virtuous livelihood is any way of living that proceeds without harming others. Because one who abides in such virtuous actions should give gifts according to their means, the text mentions "fickle wealth" and so forth. 

Because it is something to be used, "wealth" is a <term>synonym</term> <gloss>original: {bla dags}</gloss> for things to be given such as food and drink. These riches are "fickle" because they are unstable. They are "pithless" <note>without essence</note> because they can never provide true satisfaction. This teaching causes one to turn away from grasping at possessions. 

The term "Having known" means having realized this. By mentioning "monks" and so forth, the text indicates the three types of fields for giving:
1. The field of those worthy of offerings: the <term>shramanas</term> <gloss>ascetics/monks</gloss> and <term>brahmins</term>.
2. The field of compassion: the poor.
3. The field of benefactors <note>this refers to those who have previously helped the individual, such as parents</note>.

<summary>This page defines the three non-virtuous mental actions and explains why intoxicants are prohibited separately from the ten main paths of action. It also discusses the nature of wealth as unstable and categorizes the different types of beings worthy of receiving charity.</summary>
<keywords>covetousness, malice, wrong view, alcohol, virtuous livelihood, giving, field of merit, wealth, ethics</keywords>

དགེ་བ་ནི་དེ་མ་བསྐྱེད་པ་སྐྱེད་ཅིང་མི་ཉམས་པར་བྱེད་པའོ། །བསྒྲུབ་པར་བྱ་བའི་ལམ་སྟོན་པ་ནི། བདེ་གཤེགས་ཞེས་རྐང་པ་གཉིས་སོ། །མི་མ་ཡིན་པས་བསྒྲུབ་པར་མི་ནུས་པ་ནི། ལམ་དེ་ཞེས་རྐང་པ་གཉིས་སོ། །མི་རྣམས་ལམ་བསྒྲུབ་པ་ལ་སྦྱར་བ་ནི། མིའི་དངོས་པོ་

The virtue of the supreme seed of awakening <term>bodhicitta</term> <gloss>the mind of enlightenment</gloss> is what produces this path. As it is said: "Noble son, the mind of awakening is like the seed of all the Buddha's qualities."

Virtue is what produces the mind of awakening if it has not been produced, and prevents it from declining. The teaching on the path to be accomplished begins with "The Sugatas" <gloss>the Bliss-Gone Ones or Buddhas</gloss> and consists of two lines. The fact that non-humans are unable to accomplish this is explained in the two lines beginning with "That path." The application of humans to the accomplishment of the path begins with "The human condition" and consists of two lines.

Regarding the entry point to the path, which is mindfulness of impermanence, momentary impermanence is explained in the two lines beginning with "A lamp." Sudden impermanence is explained in the single stanza beginning with "This." The impermanence of the continuum is explained in the single stanza beginning with "The summer heat."

The place for accomplishment is explained in the single stanza beginning with "The moon's." The companions for accomplishment are explained in the single stanza beginning with "Forest glade." བཞི་ཞིག་བཞུགས། སྒོ་སྒོའི་ལྷ་ཁང་དང་ཡོན་བདག་མ་མཆིས་པའི་ལྷ་ཁང་ཆུང་ངུ་ནི་བརྒྱ་ལྷག་ཙམ་བཞུགས། དགེ་འདུན་ཉི་ཤུ་ཙམ་བཞུགས། ཀམ་ཤེད་དང་ཕོ་ཉ་དང་། བེ་རྒ་འདྲ་དང་། ཨོ་རྒུ་ཡན་ཆད་ཇི་ལ་མན་ཆད་སྐུ་མཁར་གྱི་ནང་དང་། སླད་རོལ་གྱི་མཚར་ཡན་ཆད་ན་གཙུག་ལག་ཁང་ཆེན་པོ་ཉི་ཤུ་
རྩ་གསུམ་བཞུགས། གཙུག་ལག་ཁང་འབྲིང་ནི་ཉི་ཤུ་རྩ་གཅིག་བཞུགས། གཙུག་ལག་ཁང་ཆུང་ངུ་ཉི་ཤུ་རྩ་གསུམ་ཙམ་བཞུགས། སྒོ་སྒོའི་མཆོད་པའི་ལྷ་ཁང་ཆུང་ངུ་དང་(ཆོད་,མཆོད་)རྟེན་ཆུང་ངུ་ནི་སྤྱིར་བརྒྱད་བརྒྱ་སུམ་ཅུ་རྩ་དགུ་བཞུགས། དགེ་འདུན་སྡེ་གཉིས་ལས་རྐྱེན་པ་དང་། སྒོ་འཚོ་
ཡན་ཆད་སྤྱིར་བཞི་བརྒྱ་སུམ་ཅུ་རྩ་བརྒྱད་བཞུགས། གྱིལ་ཀྱང་མན་ཆད་ཀོང་ཤེང་དང་། དུརྱ་ཡན་ཆད་སྐུ་མཁར་གྱི་ནང་དང་། སླད་རོལ་གྱི་ཚར་ཡན་ཆད་ན་གཙུག་ལག་ཁང་ཆེན་པོ་བཅོ་ལྔ་ཙམ་བཞུགས། སྒོ་སྒོའི་ལྷ་ཁང་ཆུང་ངུ་དང་། ཡོན་བདག་མ་མཆིས་པའི་ལྷ་ཁང་ཆུང་ངུ་དང་། མཆོད་
རྟེན་ཡན་ཆད་བཞུགས། དགེ་འདུན་སྡེ་གཉིས་ལས་རྐྱེན་པ་དང་། སྒོ་འཚོ་ཡན་ཆད་སྤྱིར་དགུ་བརྒྱ་དྲུག་ཅུ་རྩ་གསུམ་བཞུགས། རྒྱལ་པོ་ས་ནུའི་ཚ་པོ་རྒྱལ་པོ་བི་ཛ་ཡ་སཾ་བྷ་བ་ཞེས་བགྱི་བའི་ཚེ། ཐོག་མ་ལི་ཡུལ་དུ་ཆོས་བྱུང་སྟེ་བརྩིས་ན་ཁྱི་ལོའི་ཤོལ་བོར་བའི་སྟོན་ཟླ་ཐ་{ཆུངས་,ཆུང་}ཡན་ཆད་
དགུང་ལོ་སྟོང་ཉིས་བརྒྱ་ལྔ་བཅུ་རྩ་དྲུག་ཙམ་ལགས། འཕགས་པ་ཟླ་བའི་སྙིང་པོས་ཞུས་པ་དང་། ལྷ་མོ་དྲི་མ་མེད་པའི་འོད་ཀྱིས་ཞུས་པ་དང་། འཕགས་པ་དགྲ་བཅོམ་པ་དགེ་འདུན་འཕེལ་གྱིས་ལུང་བསྟན་པ་རྣམས་དང་མཐུན་པར་ལིའི་ཡུལ་དང་། དེར་ལི་རྗེའི་རྒྱལ་པོ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་
འཕགས་པ་རྣམས་སྤྱན་དྲངས་ནས། སངས་རྒྱས་ཀྱི་བསྟན་པ་དང་། དེའི་གཞི་གཙུག་ལག་ཁང་དང་། ལྷ་ཁང་དང་། མཆོད་རྟེན་རྣམས་ཇི་ལྟར་བཞེངས་པ་དང་། དགེ་འདུན་སྡེ་གཉིས་ཇི་ལྟར་སྤེལ་བའི་ཚུལ་རྒྱས་པར་བསྟན་པ་ལི་ཡུལ་ལུང་བསྟན་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་རྫོགས་སོ།། །།

Inside the fortresses and including the outer monuments, there are three thousand eight hundred and eighty-eight temples and stupas. In Khotan <term>U-then</term> <gloss>The ancient Kingdom of Khotan located on the Silk Road</gloss>, including those provided for by the monastic community, a count taken in the Year of the Mouse totals approximately ten thousand. Toward Molo and Meka, there are four great temples. Small temples at various gates and those without patrons number over one hundred. There are approximately twenty monastics residing there. From Kamshed, the envoys, and Berga-dra up to Orgu, and down to Jila, there are twenty-three great temples located both inside the fortresses and among the outer monuments. There are twenty-one medium-sized temples. Small temples number approximately twenty-three. Small offering temples at gates and small stupas total eight hundred and thirty-nine. Regarding the monastic community, including those supported by endowments and those living independently, there are four hundred and thirty-eight individuals. From Gyilkyang down to Kongsheng and up to Durya, including both the interior of fortresses and the outer monuments, there are approximately fifteen great temples. There are also small temples at various gates, small temples without patrons, and stupas. In the two monastic communities <note>the communities of monks and nuns</note>, including those with endowments and those living independently, there are nine hundred and sixty-three individuals. Calculating from the time when the Dharma first appeared in the Li country <note>Khotan</note> during the reign of King Vijaya Sambhava, the grandson of King Sanu, up to the final month of autumn in the intercalary Year of the Dog, approximately one thousand two hundred and fifty-six years have passed. This concludes the account known as the Prophecy of the Li Country <note>original: Li-yul lung-bstan-pa</note>, which describes how the kings of Li invited noble beings and established the Buddha's teachings, the foundations of temples and stupas, and the expansion of the two monastic communities, in accordance with the prophecies requested by the Noble Chandragarbha, the Goddess Vimalaprabha, and the Noble Arhat Sanghavardhana.

<summary>This page concludes a historical and statistical record of Buddhist institutions in Khotan, providing a census of temples, stupas, and monastics. It traces the history of the region's conversion back over 1,200 years to King Vijaya Sambhava.</summary>
<keywords>Khotan, Li-yul, Vijaya Sambhava, census, Buddhist temples, stupas, monastic community, Prophecy of the Li Country</keywords>
